title: PMF: normalize, select, add
description: A probability mass function gives a separate probability to each allowed discrete value. Total probability is 1.
recognize: A table of P(X = x) or a formula with an unknown constant c.
The question asks for a set of values, such as X ≥ 3 or X being even.

recipe.title: List the support
recipe.body: The support is the list of values X can actually take. Values outside it have probability 0.

recipe.title: Find any missing constant
recipe.body: Add all masses and set their sum equal to 1. Check every mass is nonnegative.

recipe.title: Translate the event
recipe.body: Write the allowed values satisfying the requested inequality before adding anything.
recipe.formula: X ≥ a → retain each support value x ≥ a

recipe.title: Add their masses
recipe.body: Different values of one random variable cannot happen together, so their probabilities add.
recipe.formula: P(X ∈ A) = Σ over x ∈ A of p(x)

pitfalls: A formula with c is not a finished PMF until c is determined.
The number of selected values is not the probability unless all masses are equal.

title: Discrete CDF: accumulate and subtract jumps
description: F(x) means P(X ≤ x), including all mass at x. A point probability is the jump in F at that point.
recognize: A staircase or piecewise constant F(x).
Strict and inclusive endpoints matter because individual discrete points can have positive probability.

recipe.title: Read the CDF carefully
recipe.body: For F(x), choose the piece whose interval contains x. At a jump use the value on the right because the CDF includes X = x.

recipe.title: Recover point masses if useful
recipe.body: Subtract the cumulative probability just before a jump from the value at the jump.

recipe.title: Match the endpoints
recipe.body: Exclude a lower endpoint with F(a); include it by subtracting F(a⁻).
recipe.formula: P(a < X ≤ b) = F(b) − F(a); P(a ≤ X ≤ b) = F(b) − F(a⁻)

recipe.title: Handle tails with a complement
recipe.body: To include a discrete lower endpoint, subtract only the mass strictly below it. For integer X, F(a⁻) = F(a − 1).

pitfalls: F(a) is cumulative, not P(X = a).
For discrete X, P(X ≥ a) usually differs from P(X > a).

title: A function of X: find the original values
description: For Y = g(X), convert the event about Y into the support values of X that produce it, then add their probabilities.
recognize: An absolute value, square, or other definition Y = g(X).
Different X values can produce the same Y value.

recipe.title: Write the support and masses
recipe.body: If supplied a CDF, first recover each mass from its jump.

recipe.title: Map every support value
recipe.body: Evaluate g(x) for each possible x. Do not lose values that map to the same answer.

recipe.title: Select the requested event
recipe.body: Retain each x whose g(x) satisfies the condition on Y.

recipe.title: Add and, if needed, condition
recipe.body: Add the selected X masses. If given B, keep only selected values also in B and divide by P(B).
recipe.formula: P(Y ∈ A | B) = Σ selected masses in B / P(B)

refs.label: Random variables assign numbers to outcomes

pitfalls: Squaring or taking an absolute value is not one-to-one.
Transform the event first; do not substitute a transformed number into the original CDF without justification.

title: Binomial: count successes in n trials
description: Use a binomial model when counting successes in a fixed number of independent trials with one constant success probability.
recognize: Fixed n, two outcomes per trial, independent trials, same p each time.
Exactly k successes, at most k, or at least k among n attempts.

recipe.title: Check all four assumptions
recipe.body: Success is whichever event you are counting; it can be an undesirable event such as a defect.

recipe.title: Write the single-count probability
recipe.body: Choose which k trials succeed, multiply their success probabilities, and multiply failures for the remaining trials.

recipe.title: Translate the range
recipe.body: Sum the masses for the integer counts in the event. For at least one, subtract zero successes.
recipe.formula: P(a ≤ X ≤ b) = Σ from k=a to b b(k); P(X ≥ 1) = 1 − (1 − p)ⁿ

recipe.title: Apply any given condition
recipe.body: The denominator is the probability of the stated given event. Intersect the requested event with it before summing.

refs.label: Exact count and at least one

pitfalls: Without replacement usually breaks independence and constant p.
Different success probabilities across trials are not an ordinary binomial model.
Do not forget C(n,k); it counts all possible orders.

title: Geometric: first success, tails, and memorylessness
description: Here the geometric variable counts trials until the first success, so values start at 1. Let q = 1 − p.
recognize: Repeated independent attempts stop at the first success.
Each attempt has the same success probability p.

recipe.title: Confirm what is counted
recipe.body: This course counts the successful trial, rather than only failures before success.

recipe.title: Describe the failure sequence
recipe.body: First success at k requires k − 1 failures then one success. Waiting beyond n requires n failures.
recipe.formula: P(T = k) = qᵏ⁻¹p; P(T > n) = qⁿ

recipe.title: Convert ranges to tails
recipe.body: For an inclusive range a to b, survive through a − 1 attempts and subtract surviving through b.

recipe.title: Process the given event
recipe.body: After known failures, the future is fresh if p stays constant. A condition such as T ≤ b is instead a truncation and requires a probability ratio.
recipe.formula: P(T > s+t | T > s) = qᵗ; P(A | B) = P(A ∩ B) / P(B)

pitfalls: P(T ≥ n) = qⁿ⁻¹, while P(T > n) = qⁿ.
Do not multiply in failures already known from the condition.
Memorylessness does not apply to a changed success chance or a guaranteed final success.

title: Guaranteed final attempt: count only earlier failures
description: A guaranteed reward at attempt m changes the success probability, so the whole waiting time is not geometric. Earlier attempts still follow the first-success pattern.
recognize: A reward is guaranteed on a specified attempt if all earlier attempts fail.
A finite maximum number of attempts.

recipe.title: Separate ordinary and guaranteed attempts
recipe.body: Before the cap use p; at the cap success has probability 1.
recipe.formula: P(T = k) = qᵏ⁻¹p for k < m

recipe.title: Reach the guaranteed attempt
recipe.body: The event T = m requires all m − 1 earlier ordinary attempts to fail.

recipe.title: Use the given information
recipe.body: If the first s attempts are known failures, cancel them from numerator and denominator.
recipe.formula: P(T = m | T > s) = qᵐ⁻¹ / qˢ = qᵐ⁻¹⁻ˢ

recipe.title: Count only failures that remain
recipe.body: Do not multiply by p on the guaranteed attempt because its success chance is 1.

refs.label: A pity system is not geometric

pitfalls: Multiplying by ordinary p at the guaranteed attempt is wrong.
The failure exponent stops at m − 1, not m.

title: Poisson: scale the rate to the interval
description: A Poisson variable counts events in an interval. λ is the expected count for that exact interval.
recognize: A count of arrivals, requests, or alerts during a time interval.
A Poisson or constant-rate arrival model is stated.

recipe.title: Match the units
recipe.body: Convert the interval into the rate units before multiplying.

recipe.title: Write one count probability
recipe.body: The count k is a nonnegative integer and 0! = 1.

recipe.title: Sum a short range or use a complement
recipe.body: For at least a small number, subtract counts below it; this avoids an infinite sum.
recipe.formula: P(X ≥ r) = 1 − Σ from k=0 to r−1 e⁻λ λᵏ/k!

recipe.title: Apply any condition
recipe.body: If given X ≥ 1, divide the desired positive-count mass by 1 − e⁻λ.
recipe.formula: P(a ≤ X ≤ b | X ≥ 1) = Σ from k=a to b P(X = k) / (1 − e⁻λ), a ≥ 1

pitfalls: An hourly rate is not the mean for a 25-minute or 90-minute interval.
Counts that cluster strongly or a rate that changes over time may violate the model.

title: Poisson approximation to rare binomial events
description: The exact model is binomial when there are n independent trials with common p. For large n and small p, approximate it with Poisson(np).
recognize: Many independent items and a small defect or loss probability.
The question explicitly requests a Poisson approximation.

recipe.title: State the exact model
recipe.body: Do not relabel a fixed-trial experiment as exactly Poisson.

recipe.title: Check whether approximation is sensible
recipe.body: The lecture gives n ≥ 50 and p ≤ 0.10 as a classroom guide, with np not too large; this is not a universal cutoff.

recipe.title: Preserve the expected count
recipe.body: Use np for the new Poisson parameter, rather than p alone.

recipe.title: Use the same event and mark approximation
recipe.body: Evaluate the requested count or range under Y. For a conditional probability, approximate both numerator and denominator consistently.

pitfalls: The Poisson answer is approximate, not exact.
Do not use λ = p or forget n.
For conditional questions, approximating only one part gives an inconsistent ratio.

title: Bernoulli: one yes-or-no trial
description: A Bernoulli variable encodes one outcome as 1 and its alternative as 0.
recognize: One user, one toss, or one trial with a binary outcome.
X equals 1 for the event and 0 otherwise.

recipe.title: Choose the event called success
recipe.body: Success simply means the event coded 1, whether or not it is desirable.
recipe.formula: X = 1 for success; X = 0 for failure

recipe.title: Assign the success probability
recipe.body: Read p directly from the chance of the event coded 1.

recipe.title: Complete the PMF
recipe.body: There are only two values, so the other mass is its complement.

pitfalls: Counting successes among several trials gives binomial, not a single Bernoulli variable.
